1 A landscape of KVM management frontends

virsh, virt-manager, Cockpit machines, and WebVirtCloud generally manage QEMU/KVM through libvirt, but not every tool uses the same API. Proxmox VE has its own management stack, while virt-builder primarily builds offline images. Even tools that use libvirt must connect to the same host and URI to see the same domains.

GUI, CLI, and IaC tools can operate on the same domain, but not every operation has an equivalent entry point. When mixing tools, establish resource ownership so the next Terraform/NixVirt apply does not overwrite manual edits. Do not assume that Boxes session/Flatpak instances share resources with the host’s system libvirt instance.
Graphical interface on a local desktop
Visual management of a single host, development, and debugging
Remote management, multiple hosts, and multi-user collaboration
Desktop GUI tools run in the local desktop environment of a workstation or server and operate libvirt directly through a graphical interface.
2.1 GNOME Boxes: the simplest graphical KVM client

GNOME Boxes is the GNOME desktop environment’s virtualization tool, designed to work with "zero configuration". The original notes were written in the GNOME 49 era; this article retains the feature overview without calling 49.0 the current latest version. Its current official focus is local virtual machines; GNOME Connections handles remote desktops.
Automatically detects ISO images and recommends optimal VM settings through osinfo-db
Supports Express Installation for mainstream operating systems (Fedora/Ubuntu/Debian/Windows)
Clipboard sharing, drag-and-drop files, USB redirection, and dynamic resolution adjustment
Enabled for some supported guest operating systems
Built-in VNC/spice client can connect to remote virtual machines

Boxes usually manages resources in the user session scope; verify the URI for the particular package or Flatpak instance. It does not provide the full system-level management interfaces available in tools such as virt-manager. However, session scope alone does not mean every lifecycle feature is necessarily unavailable.
No TCG fallback: if the CPU lacks VT-x/AMD-V, Boxes refuses to work rather than falling back to software emulation
Overwrites custom CPU settings: if you manually set host-passthrough, which is needed for nested virtualization, Boxes resets it on the next start
No snapshots with UEFI: snapshot functionality for EFI virtual machines has long-standing limitations
No fine-grained hardware tuning: no precise CPU model configuration, multiple virtual disks, or complex device layouts
Best suited to: beginners quickly trying other Linux distributions, lightweight virtualization for desktop users, and simple Windows virtual machines

Boxes vs virt-manager
If KVM virtualization were a way of getting around:
GNOME Boxes is a bicycle: quick to learn and good for short trips, but unable to carry heavy loads
virt-manager is a repair workshop: fully equipped to dismantle and assemble every part, but with a learning curve
When Boxes is no longer sufficient, you can open the same virtual machine in virt-manager without losing any data.
virt-viewer is not a virtual-machine manager; it is purely a desktop console client. It does one thing: connect to a virtual machine’s graphical console.

virt-manager includes virt-viewer’s functionality, essentially using the same SPICE/VNC client libraries. If virt-manager is already open, you do not need to launch virt-viewer separately. If you only need a console connection and do not want to launch the full virt-manager application, virt-viewer is lighter. For details, see 04 Graphical KVM management.

The following retains an overview of each platform’s features; version numbers and earlier release dates are historical context only. Cluster HA, migration, snapshots, and backups all require additional storage, quorum, or compatibility conditions. QEMU live migration differs from LXC migration: container migration involving a restart should not be described as zero-downtime migration of memory state. Before deployment, review publicly exposed management UI listeners, default accounts, and permissions.
Web management platforms provide graphical controls through a browser. Their key advantages are remote access and multi-user collaboration, without installing a client on the management machine.

Cockpit is a lightweight web-based server management tool maintained by Red Hat, running on port 9090 by default. The cockpit-machines plugin provides common libvirt virtual-machine management functions; exact capabilities vary with the plugin version.
Visit https://<服务器IP>:9090 and sign in with a system account.
VNC or serial console, with no additional client required
Add/remove virtual disks and manage storage pools
Add vNICs, select source mode, and manage bridges
Adjust vCPUs and memory while running
Search for and download OS images directly when creating a VM
Upgrade to the PatternFly 6 UI framework (v330) for a more modern interface
Source mode selection for virtual network interfaces (v333), enabling finer network control
Enhanced VNC and serial consoles (v336), including scaling controls
Lightweight: adds only a web frontend, without changing the underlying KVM architecture
Integrated server management: manages disks, networking, logs, terminals, and containers as well as VMs; containers require cockpit-podman
Backed by Red Hat: a default component of Fedora Server and RHEL, with ongoing active maintenance
Multiple hosts: Cockpit can connect to and manage multiple servers
Cannot create bridges from the web UI; the CLI is required

Storage pool creation and selection depend on the cockpit-machines version and backend. Check the current interface and documentation rather than treating historical limitations as permanent omissions.
ISO downloads sometimes fail to find an image; downloading manually is recommended
Advanced operations still require the virsh CLI
Best suited to: managing one or more KVM hosts, general server management requiring a web UI, and users who do not want to install a dedicated virtualization OS.
3.2 Proxmox VE: a complete virtualization platform

Proxmox Virtual Environment (Proxmox VE) is more than a frontend: it is a complete Type-1 virtualization operating system, based on Debian and integrating a web UI, KVM virtualization, LXC containers, ZFS storage, clustering, and backup systems.
Not an APT package: it is a complete OS:

Installation methods
Proxmox VE is a complete host platform, with both an official ISO installation method and a package-based route on supported Debian systems. The ISO generally involves disk layout changes and reinstallation, so it should not be treated as an ordinary GUI application for an existing host. The original notes’ 8.4 / Debian 12 combination is a historical example. For current deployments, check the installation documentation and support lifecycle of the selected release.
KVM full virtualization + LXC containers, managed together
Corosync-based multi-host clusters, with capacity depending on version, resources, and quorum design, and centralized web management
Native ZFS integration, Ceph distributed storage, NFS/iSCSI/LVM/Gluster
Both KVM and LXC support live migration
Built-in vzdump snapshot backups + incremental, deduplicated backups with Proxmox Backup Server (PBS)
Software-defined networking (VXLAN, EVPN) with multi-tenant isolation
Local users, LDAP/AD, OpenID Connect, and two-factor authentication
Container and virtual-machine templates for rapid clone deployment
Enhanced live migration for a more stable migration process
Improved backup integration and closer coordination with Proxmox Backup Server
Kernel updated to the 6.8 series, supporting newer hardware
Enterprise-grade features with a free community edition under the AGPL license
The web UI covers full platform management; the feature set depends on the platform version
A large community ecosystem with extensive tutorials and documentation
Unified management of both virtual machines and containers
Requires replacing the operating system or installing an additional layer on Debian
Heavier than Cockpit; even a single-host deployment requires the complete Proxmox stack
Clusters need a stable network because Corosync is sensitive to latency
Enterprise support requires a paid subscription
Best suited to: a first choice for homelabs, virtualization in small and medium-sized businesses, environments needing clustering and high availability, and users migrating from VMware.

oVirt is the upstream open-source project for Red Hat Virtualization (RHV), positioned as a KVM alternative with a role similar to VMware vSphere. It uses a centralized management engine: one oVirt Engine manages multiple KVM host nodes.

Slower development
The official oVirt release records provide historical change notes for 4.5.7. Do not infer that maintenance has stopped, or that this is the only update, from a single release interval. Evaluate the selected release, host OS support, upgrade path, documentation, and actual community maintenance status, rather than calling a historical version current.
New CPU support: AMD EPYC Milan/Rome/Genoa, Intel Sapphire Rapids, and IBM POWER10
Full migration of Java code to Java 21
Fix for CVE-2024-7259, an administrator-password disclosure vulnerability
A centralized Engine manages tens to hundreds of KVM nodes
Rapid template-based VM deployment, with versioning and inheritance
An abstract storage layer supporting NFS/iSCSI/FC/Gluster
Supports simultaneous live migration of storage and compute
Role-based access control with a self-service portal
Virtual-machine affinity and anti-affinity rules control whether VMs run on the same or different hosts
A vSphere-style management experience: data center → cluster → host → VM
Upstream of RHV, compatible with the Red Hat ecosystem
Complex deployment: install the Engine, configure storage domains, and add hosts
The Java engine is relatively heavy and needs substantial resources
Community development has slowed, with an uncertain long-term outlook
Centered on RHEL/CentOS, with limited Debian-family support
Best suited to: existing RHV users, large enterprise data centers with dozens or more KVM hosts, and environments needing a vSphere-like management model.

Red Hat’s new direction Red Hat’s current primary virtualization offering is OpenShift Virtualization, based on KubeVart, which runs virtual machines as Kubernetes workloads on OpenShift clusters. If you are planning new enterprise virtualization infrastructure, consider evaluating both Proxmox VE and OpenShift Virtualization.

WebVirtCloud is an open-source web-based KVM management platform built on Python/Django. It aims to offer a Proxmox-like web management experience without replacing the operating system; it can be installed directly on an existing Linux server.
Core technology stack: Python >= 3.11, Django 4.2 LTS, libvirt, noVNC
Create, delete, update, power on/off, suspend/resume, and force reboot
Adjust vCPUs and memory while running, with ballooning support, and expand disks
Directory storage, LVM, Ceph, NFS, and dedicated ISO pools
NAT virtual networks, bridged networks, physical interface passthrough, NIC QoS, and NWFilter
Supports cloud-init data sources to automate initial VM configuration
Role-based access control: super administrators, regular administrators, and regular users
Supports migration modes including compression, auto-converge, and post-copy
VMs are visible in both the web interface and virsh
Activity: the retspen/webvirtcloud fork remained active on GitHub through 2025-2026, with support for Ubuntu 26.04/24.04/22.04 and Debian.
No OS replacement; can be added to an existing server
Multiple users and hosts, suitable for team collaboration
A complete REST API for automation integrations
Less feature depth than Proxmox VE, with no built-in cluster HA or integrated backup server
Remote host management relies on SSH connections, so performance is affected by the network

Best suited to: teams wanting to add web management to existing Linux servers, environments needing simple multi-tenant web management, and DevOps workflows that orchestrate KVM resources through an API.
3.5 Kimchi / Wok: historical projects and checking maintenance status
Kimchi is an HTML5-based KVM management tool started by IBM in 2014. Wok is the CherryPy-based web framework used by Kimchi.
The v2.5 release cited in the original notes is historical. Before deployment, check repository releases, archival status, and security maintenance.
The status of the original sponsorship does not mean that development has stopped on every branch today; evaluate the specific repository and its dependencies.
Last activity in the Kimchi repository was in January 2023
Last activity in the Wok repository was in June 2021
Not recommended for any new deployment; included here only as historical background
If you are evaluating web-based KVM management, choose from Cockpit, Proxmox VE, and WebVirtCloud rather than Kimchi/Wok.
Desktop GUIs and web UIs suit interactive work, but CLI and automation tools are indispensable in the following scenarios:
Bulk management: operating on hundreds of virtual machines at once
Scripting/CI/CD: integrating VM creation and destruction into automated pipelines
Infrastructure as Code: defining virtualization infrastructure declaratively
Headless servers: remote hosts without a desktop environment or browser
virsh is the official command-line tool from the libvirt project and the low-level foundation for all other frontends. Anything graphical frontends can do, virsh can do.
For detailed virsh usage, see 03 KVM CLI management. Here are its key characteristics:
Versatility: one command manages every backend supported by libvirt, including KVM, Xen, LXC, and QEMU
Remote capabilities: manage virtualization on remote hosts through -c qemu+ssh://
Script-friendly: output can be processed with grep/awk/jq, making it suitable for automation
Native XML: operates directly on libvirt XML definitions, without an intervening abstraction layer

virt-install is part of the virt-manager project and is dedicated to creating virtual machines from the command line. It can generate domains and drive installation or import workflows, often including define/start. It also handles installation media and guest defaults, so it is not simply an alias for two commands.
For more virt-install usage, see 04 Graphical KVM management, which covers both virt-manager and virt-install.

First use --list/--notes to choose a template that actually exists, then pin and verify its source. Password files should have 0600 permissions and be supplied through a secure runtime mechanism. Avoid plaintext passwords in command arguments or committing password files to a repository. Building a template neither creates a domain nor verifies behavior after boot.
virt-builder comes from the libguestfs project and can quickly build virtual-machine images from predefined templates:

virt-builder’s strengths are repeatability and automation. Pinning template versions, checksums, repositories, and customization inputs improves repeatability, but randomized identities, timestamps, and mutable software repositories mean the same command does not guarantee byte-identical output. It is a natural fit for CI/CD pipelines.

Terraform’s dmacvicar/libvirt provider brings KVM virtualization into Infrastructure as Code:

Terraform suits virtualization environments that need declarative management, version control, and collaborative review. If you already use Terraform to manage cloud resources, extending it to local KVM hosts is a natural step.

Quick VM creation for beginners and desktop experimentation
General server management + web-based VM management
Homelabs / production in small and medium-sized businesses
(Historical option; check maintenance and security status before deployment)
GNOME Boxes → switch to virt-manager if it is insufficient
Move seamlessly from simple to advanced tools
Cockpit for everyday checks, virsh for advanced operations
A complete, free solution for clustering, backups, containers, and ZFS
Proxmox VE (recommended) / oVirt (with prior RHV experience)
Active Proxmox community and low cost
Assess migration costs based on maintenance, compatibility, and the organization’s existing platform

When combining tools, record the host, URI, storage ownership, and definition ownership. System and session instances have different resources; Proxmox is not managed through virsh. Manual GUI edits can drift from IaC definitions. Feed changes back into the configuration that owns the resource and retain recovery information.

Combine interfaces as needed while preserving definition ownership
Tools connected to the same libvirt instance can work together, provided resource ownership and synchronization of changes are clear:
Use Cockpit for everyday monitoring and simple operations, with convenient remote web access
Use virsh for advanced configuration and scripted bulk operations
Use virt-manager for complex desktop-side debugging and PCI passthrough configuration
Use cloud-init + Terraform for highly consistent environment cloning and IaC management
Concurrent operations and IaC/GUI state drift can still conflict. Do not run simultaneous jobs that modify the same domain, network, or disk.
Getting started: install GNOME Boxes and begin with a local test VM. The time required depends on image downloads, hardware, and the installation process
Expanding your capabilities: when Boxes is no longer enough, install virt-manager and learn basic virsh commands
Server use: deploy Cockpit for web management and use virsh for deeper operations
Homelab/production: evaluate complete platforms such as Proxmox VE, including their requirements for reinstallation, storage, backups, and quorum
Existing enterprise KVM: continue using oVirt if already deployed; evaluate OpenShift Virtualization for new environments
DevOps/cloud-native: choose cloud-init, Terraform, NixVirt, or other automation tools according to the existing platform
What to avoid: first check the current maintenance, dependencies, and security fixes of historical options such as Kimchi/Wok; do not use them for new deployments if support is lacking

The key insight Choosing a KVM management frontend is fundamentally a user-experience decision rather than a technical one: they share the same backend. Select based on four dimensions: team skills, management scale, the need for web access, and willingness to replace the OS, rather than comparing underlying capabilities.
